passage:
Day 1. Santosh arrived at the university in Helsinki and met his lab partner, Hansa, who listened to his introduction with an almost blank face and said, "Good." He felt his stomach sink, sure that she disliked him.
Day 4. Back home, everyone shows what they think on their face, so he read her calm expression as coldness. In the lab she hardly smiled, but she checked his calculations twice and stayed late to help.
Day 10. Santosh asked her directly, "Are you okay working with me? I can't tell." Hansa looked surprised. "Very much. I'm listening. A calm face is how I show respect here." They both laughed.

qa.q: Where did Santosh meet his lab partner?
qa.a: He met her at the university in Helsinki.

qa.q: What did Santosh feel when Hansa answered with an almost blank face?
qa.a: He felt anxious and rejected, and he took her calm face as a sign she disliked him.

qa.q: What did Santosh do that cleared things up?
qa.a: He asked Hansa directly whether she was okay working with him, instead of relying on stereotypes or guesses.

qa.q: How might Hansa have felt when Santosh read her calm face as coldness?
qa.a: She may have been surprised and a little sorry, since she was showing respect and care through help and listening, not through open expression.

grounding: A young adult abroad reads a restrained face as coldness, then learns by asking that it means respect and calm.

passage: "When I started at the plant in Osaka thirty years ago, Kalyani, I thought my supervisor hated me," Arnab said, pouring tea for his niece, who was packing for her exchange year. "Mr Tanaka never smiled when I proposed anything. He nodded once, wrote something down and said 'I will consider it.' I lay awake at night reading that as failure." He chuckled. "Months later I learned he put my ideas in the monthly meeting, and his still face was how he listened. A colleague explained it. I could have asked him myself, and saved myself many nights." Kalyani looked up. "So I should ask?" "Politely and directly, yes. And don't decide about a whole country from one face."

qa.q: Where did Arnab start working thirty years ago?
qa.a: He started at the plant in Osaka.

qa.q: What did Arnab feel about his supervisor's still face at first?
qa.a: He felt anxious and rejected, sure that he was failing and that his supervisor hated him.

qa.q: What advice does Arnab give Kalyani?
qa.a: To ask politely and directly when she can't read a face abroad, and not to judge a whole country from one expression.

qa.q: How might Mr Tanaka have seen his own behaviour?
qa.a: He may have thought he was being respectful and attentive by listening quietly and taking the ideas to the meeting.

grounding: A young adult working abroad finds a restrained face can mean respect, not coldness, and asking directly avoids stereotypes.

passage:
Sachin had been in Munich for three months on his engineering exchange. The group project was due in two days, and his lab partner Thomas had barely reacted all week.
When Sachin showed him the finished model, Thomas looked at it for ten seconds, nodded once and said, "Good." No smile. No "wow." Then he went back to his laptop.
Sachin's stomach sank. Back home, his friends would have shouted and clapped. Was Thomas annoyed? Did he think it was bad?
With the deadline so close, he couldn't afford guessing. After the lab emptied, he asked, "Thomas, honestly, are you happy with the model? You didn't say much."
Thomas looked surprised. "I'm very happy. It's excellent. In my family, 'good' is a big compliment. We don't jump around." He paused. "You've been worried?"
"A bit."
Thomas smiled, a small one. "I'll try to say 'excellent' more."

qa.q: How many days until the project was due?
qa.a: Two days.

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling when Thomas only said "Good"?
qa.a: Sachin felt anxious and deflated, worried that Thomas was annoyed or thought the model was bad.

qa.q: Which choice of Sachin's worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking Thomas directly worked, because his restrained face reflected his family's style, not displeasure, and guessing would have wasted time.

qa.q: How did Thomas see his own reaction?
qa.a: For Thomas, a nod and "good" was a big compliment, so he was surprised Sachin had been worried.

grounding: The scene shows a young adult abroad misreading a restrained face as coldness and asking directly instead of relying on stereotypes.

passage:
In their Bengaluru office, Uday pitched his idea for the new app feature with full energy: hands moving, voice rising, big smile. His teammates laughed and nodded along.
Lalremsiami, the senior designer, listened with a calm, still face. She didn't smile or nod. She took a few notes.
Uday faltered. He finished quickly and sat down, sure she hated it.
After the meeting he almost went straight to his desk. Instead he stopped by hers. "Can I ask what you thought? I couldn't read you at all."
She looked up, surprised. "I liked it a lot. I was listening carefully." She showed him her notes, three ideas to make it better. "In my family, you stay quiet and still when someone important is speaking. It's a sign of respect."
Uday laughed. "In mine, if you're quiet, something's wrong."
"Then we'll both have to ask more."

qa.q: How many ideas did Lalremsiami write in her notes?
qa.a: Three ideas to make it better.

qa.q: What was Uday feeling when Lalremsiami kept a still face?
qa.a: Uday felt anxious and discouraged, faltering and sure she hated the idea.

qa.q: What did Uday do that avoided a misunderstanding?
qa.a: He asked Lalremsiami directly what she thought instead of assuming her calm face meant disapproval.

qa.q: How does Lalremsiami see a quiet, still face while listening?
qa.a: She sees it as a sign of respect, learned in her family, not as coldness or disinterest.

grounding: The scene shows a young adult misreading a colleague's restrained face, and asking directly revealing that it showed respect.

passage:
"Devika, I think my team lead hates me."
"Kalyani, you've been in Seoul two months. What happened?"
"Nothing happened! That's the problem. I presented my first report today. I thought it went well. And his face just... didn't move. No smile, no nod. He said 'thank you' and moved on."
Devika, in her Pune flat, put her tea down. "What about with the others?"
Kalyani thought. "Actually... same face with everyone."
"So maybe it's just his face. Or how people show things in that office. Or he's shy."
"But at home my boss says 'superb!' for everything."
"And you're not at home. Why don't you just ask him if he has any feedback?"
"That feels so direct."
"More direct than lying awake thinking he hates you?"
Kalyani laughed. "Fine."
Next day she asked. He said, quietly, "It was very clear. Please do the next one too."

qa.q: How long had Kalyani been in Seoul?
qa.a: Two months.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling after the presentation?
qa.a: Kalyani felt anxious and unsure, reading the team lead's still face as dislike.

qa.q: What did Devika suggest, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She suggested asking him directly for feedback, because a still face could be his style, office norms or shyness, not dislike.

qa.q: How did the team lead actually see Kalyani's report?
qa.a: He found it very clear and wanted her to do the next one too, though his face didn't show it.

grounding: The dialogue shows a young adult abroad misreading a restrained face as coldness, and a friend advising a direct question instead of assumptions.

passage: My first month doing my master's in Osaka, I was convinced my lab partner, Aoi, disliked me. When I presented my data at the Thursday meeting, my friends back home would have been nodding, interrupting, going "arre wah!" Aoi just sat very still, hands folded, face almost blank, and said "Thank you" at the end. I went back to my desk feeling like I'd bombed. Lakshmi, from Chennai, who had been in the lab three years, laughed when I told her. "Raghav, my grandmother keeps that exact face at weddings. For her it means respect. But don't turn one person into a whole country. Just ask her." So I did, awkwardly, by the coffee machine: "Was my presentation okay? I couldn't tell." Aoi looked surprised. "It was very clear. I was concentrating so I would not miss anything. Your graph of the enzyme curve, can you send it?" I sent it that afternoon.

qa.q: What did Aoi ask Raghav to send?
qa.a: Aoi asked for the graph of the enzyme curve.

qa.q: How did Raghav feel after the Thursday presentation?
qa.a: Raghav felt deflated and anxious, sure the talk had bombed because Aoi's face stayed almost blank; Raghav was reading home expectations onto that face.

qa.q: What advice from Lakshmi helped, and why?
qa.a: Lakshmi pointed out that a still face can mean respect, warned against turning one person into a whole country, and said to ask, which got a direct answer.

qa.q: What did the still face mean for Aoi?
qa.a: For Aoi it meant concentrating so as not to miss anything, and she actually found the presentation very clear.

grounding: It shows a young adult abroad misreading a colleague's restrained face as coldness, and asking directly instead of relying on a stereotype.
